newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-MPs condemn delay in EU ban on animal testing.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs condemn delay in EU ban on animal testing.

text.p: The European Parliament attacked the European Commission on Tuesday for delaying the introduction of a planned European Union ban on sales of cosmetics tested on animals.
The EU approved a directive in 1993 ordering member states to end the sale of all cosmetics tested on animals by 1998.

But the EU Committee on the Adaptation to Technical Progress, chaired by the Commission and made up of officials from the 15 member states, decided on March 20 to extend testing on animals until June 2000 because, it said, internationally acceptable alternative methods did not yet exist.

The Commission has warned that unless alternatives are suitably validated, exports of European cosmetics tested in this way may not be given legal approval in other countries, such as the United States.
It has also warned a blanket ban could face a challenge through the World Trade Organsation from cosmetic companies in countries like Japan and the U.S.
WTO rules allow the EU to outlaw animal-tested cosmetics manufactured domestically but not imports from third countries.
Euro-MPs adopted a critical report by German Socialist Dagmar Roth-Behrendt which accused the Commission of not pushing the cosmetics industry into finding new testing methods.

"Full implementation of the ban...will provide the greatest incentive for the industry, member states and the Commission to complete the necessary development of...non-animal alternative tests," the report said.
Animal welfare activists also condemned the EU decision saying it meant further suffering for thousands of animals.

Euro-MPs and animal welfare groups insist that using non-animal tested products will not jeopardise consumer safety or the viability of cosmetics firms because the industry can still use some 8,000 currently available ingredients to develop new products.

European consumer affairs commissioner Emma Bonino told the assembly on Monday night that the Commission planned shortly to confirm the animal test ban from 1998, but only for finished cosmetic products.
Sticking to existing products was not an entirely viable option in all cases, she said.
Science was constantly evolving and tests would therefore continue to be necessary, she said, pointing out that cosmetics accounted for only 0.03 percent of all products experimented on animals.
Bonino insisted the Commission was actively seeking alternative testing methods, financing research in this field to the tune of 12 million Ecus.
The parliament's report demanded an explicit commitment from the Commission not to try and delay the ban further beyond the year 2000.
The dispute mirrors a furious row between parliament and the Commission over the latter's repeated postponement of a planned ban on imports of fur from animals caught in steel-jawed leghold traps.
The Commission has argued for a delay in the fur import ban to give it time to reach an agreement on more humane trapping standards with Canada, Russia and the U.S., which still use the traps.
Trade commissioner Sir Leon Brittan has warned introduction of the fur ban could trigger a trade dispute.
Commissioner Bonino admitted that as it stood, the animal test ban for cosmetics posed international trade problems.
One possible solution, she suggested, would be to confine the animal test ban to cosmetics produced in the EU but leave third country imports untouched.

Last November, Britain's ecologically minded cosmetic firm The Body Shop and the European Coalition to End Animal Testing presented the Commission and European Parliament with a petition bearing more than four million signatures, calling for cosmetic tests on animals to be banned from 1998.
